reasons: Lake identity gives case_name_full as Ohio v. Robinette, court as U.S. Supreme Court, date_decided as 1996-11-18, and year as 1996.
Lake citations list official cite 519 U.S. 33, parallels 117 S. Ct. 417 and 136 L. Ed. 2d 347, and vendor-neutral cite 1996 U.S. LEXIS 6971.
Opinion text header also shows 519 U.S. 33 (1996), United States Supreme Court, decided November 18, 1996.
The opinion states the question as whether the Fourth Amendment requires advice that a lawfully seized defendant is free to go before consent to search is voluntary.
The opinion discusses Schneckloth's consent-search voluntariness rule and applies it to a traffic-stop consent search.
That supports placement under Consent Searches and the role as a key refinement/progeny case.

The opinion states: "We are here presented with the question whether the Fourth Amendment requires that a lawfully seized defendant must be advised that he is \"free to go\" before his consent to search will be recognized as voluntary. We hold that it does not."
The opinion further states that it would be unrealistic to always require officers to inform detainees they are free to go before consent may be deemed voluntary.
The opinion preserves the totality rule: consent must be voluntary under all the circumstances, so the holding is not an automatic-voluntariness rule.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: To avoid misreading, phrase as: no free-to-go advisory is a categorical Fourth Amendment prerequisite; voluntariness remains totality-of-the-circumstances.
